5.1 Calcium and Bone Metabolism

5.1.1 Roles of Calcium

Building block of bone, and helps maintain bone strength Skeletal strength Neuromuscular conduction Stimulus secretion coupling (e.g., chromaffin cells) The bones contain approximately 99.5% of the total calcium in the body.

5.1.2 Calcium in the Circulation

Circulating calcium exists in several forms.

• Ionized—biologically active (50%)

• Complexed to citrate, phosphate, etc.—biologically active (5%)

• Bound to protein, mainly albumin—inactive (45%)

In most clinical situations, direct measurement of ionized calcium concentration is unnecessary. However, it is important to adjust the measured calcium concentration for the prevailing serum albumin concentration: Adjusted Ca = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin) (where calcium is in mmol/L and albumin in g/L).

5.2 Calcium-Regulating Hormones

5.2.1 PTH and Parathyroid Glands

Parathyroid Glands

• The central function of PTH is to regulate ionized [Ca2+] levels by concerted

effects on three principal target organs: bone, intestinal mucosa, and kidney. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is an 84-amino-acid peptide secreted from four glands: the two superior glands are usually found near the posterior aspect of the thyroid capsule while the inferior glands are most often located near the inferior thyroid margin. The normal parathyroid glands weigh an average of 40 mg each. Though the parathyroid glands are usually located on the back of the thyroid, their position is variable. Some people have one or more parathyroid glands elsewhere in the neck or in the chest—actually, they may be ectopic, located throughout the neck or upper mediastinum, along the thymus descending line. Moreover, 12–15% of normal persons have a fifth parathyroid gland. The explanation resides in their embryological development. The parathyroid glands arise from the third and fourth branchial pouches. The pair of glands which is ultimately inferior develops from the third pouch with the thymus, and one of them sometimes follows the thymus gland into the superior mediastinum whereas the pair of glands which is ultimately superior develops from the fourth pouch. These ectopic parathyroid glands may pose difficulties in localization when they become the site of a pathological process: PTH secreting adenoma formation.

PTH: Biologic Effects

• On kidney—PTH has direct effects: ↑ Ca2+ reabsorption in the distal convoluted

tubes, ↓ reabsorption of phosphate in the renal proximal tubule and of bicarbonate; additionally, ⊕ the synthesis of 1,25(OH)2D3 in the proximal tubule by inducing transcription of the 1α-hydroxylase gene.

• On intestinal mucosa: the effect of PTH on intestinal calcium absorption is indirect, resulting from ↑ renal production of the intestinally active vitamin D metabolite, 1,25(OH)2D3.

• On bone: PTH ↑ both bone formation and bone resorption; with regard to calcium homeostasis, the effect of PTH on bone resorption is dominant (Fig. 5.1).

Calcitonin: Biologic Effects

Calcitonin (CT) is secreted by parafollicular C cells of the thyroid.

• On bone: CT inhibits osteoclastic-mediated bone resorption (its main function).

• On kidney: CT inhibits the reabsorption of phosphate and ↑ the renal excretion

of calcium.

5.2.3 Vitamin D and Its Metabolites

The main function of vitamin D metabolites is the regulation of calcium and phosphate homeostasis, which occurs in conjunction with PTH. The gut, kidney, and bone are the principal target tissues for this regulation.

5.2.3.1 25OH Vitamin D (25OHD)

This is the main storage form of vitamin D, and the measurement of “total vitamin D” is the most clinically useful measure of vitamin D status. Internationally, there remains controversy around a “normal” or “optimal” concentration of vitamin D. Levels over 50 nmol/L are generally accepted as satisfactory and values <25 nmol/L representing deficiency. Low levels of 25OHD can result from a variety of causes (see Vitamin D deficiency). The major pathologic complication of vitamin D deficiency is rickets (in children) or osteomalacia (in adults), which results mainly from the deficiency of calcium and phosphate required for bone mineralization. Vitamin D3 is hydroxylated in the liver to form 25-hydroxycholecalciferol [25(OH)D3]. Another hydroxylation reaction occurs in the kidneys, stimulated by PTH, where 25(OH)D3 is converted to the biologically active form 1α,25(OH)2D3 (calcitriol) (see Fig. 5.2). Control of metabolism is exerted primarily at the level of the kidney where low serum phosphate, low serum calcium, and high PTH levels favor production of 1,25(OH)2D, whereas fibroblast-derived growth factor 23 (FGF23), high serum calcium and phosphate, and 1,25(OH)2D inhibit 1,25(OH)2D

5.3 Regulation of Parathyroid Hormone Secretion

PTH secretion is regulated by the serum Ca2+ through negative feedback. The extracellular calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), expressed on the parathyroid cell senses changes in extracellular calcium—so, ↓ Ca2+ →↑ PTH secretion, while ↑ levels of Ca2+ →↓ PTH secretion (Fig. 5.3). Besides calcium, there are other several regulators of PTH secretion. Hypermagnesemia inhibits PTH, while conversely, moderate hypomagnesemia can stimulate PTH secretion, even though prolonged depletion of

Hypercalcemia

5.4.1 Epidemiology and Etiology

Hypercalcemia is found in 5% of hospital patients and in 0.5% of the general population. Many different disease states can lead to hypercalcemia (see Table 5.1).

5.4.2 Investigation of Hypercalcemia

5.4.2.1 Confirm the Diagnosis

Serum calcium (adjusted for albumin)/Ca2+.

5.4.2.2 Determine the Cause

The first step in the differential diagnosis is determination of intact PTH. As a practical matter, the categories for differential diagnosis of hypercalcemia are (primary) hyperparathyroidism and everything else. If the PTH level is high, and thus inappropriate for hypercalcemia, little further workup is required. This combination suggests parathyroid overactivity, primary hyperparathyroidism or rarely, tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Conversely, if hypercalcemia has a non-parathyroid basis, then PTH will be suppressed ⇒ a search for other entities (see Table 5.1) must be conducted.

5.5 Primary Hyperparathyroidism

Hyperparathyroidism is by far the most common cause of hypercalcemia. Primary hyperparathyroidism results from excessive, autonomic secretion of PTH. Primary hyperparathyroidism is caused by a single parathyroid adenoma in about 80% of cases and by primary hyperplasia of the parathyroids in 10–15%. Parathyroid carcinoma is a rare cause of hyperparathyroidism, accounting for 1–2% of cases. Primary hyperparathyroidism can be associated with genetic abnormalities and can occur as part of

• MEN type 1: parathyroid hyperplasia (primary hyperparathyroidism) + pancreatic tumors + pituitary tumors

• MEN type 2a: medullary carcinoma of the thyroid + pheochromocytoma + parathyroid hyperplasia

5.5 Primary Hyperparathyroidism

95

5.5.1 Clinical Features

The typical clinical presentation of primary hyperparathyroidism has evolved considerably over the past few decades. As the disease continues to be detected primarily by multiphasic screening that includes determination of serum calcium levels, there has been a marked reduction in the frequency of the classic signs and symptoms of primary hyperparathyroidism, which are renal disease (stones, decreased renal function, and occasionally nephrocalcinosis) and the classic hyperparathyroid bone disease-osteitis fibrosa cystica. In fact, about 85% of patients presenting today have neither bone nor renal manifestations of hyperparathyroidism and are regarded as asymptomatic or at most minimally symptomatic.

5.5.1.1 Bone Disease

• Osteitis fibrosa cystica, the classic bone disease of hyperparathyroidism, causing

bone pain and sometimes pathologic fractures; rare, usually with tertiary hyperparathyroidism; histologically, there is an increase in the number of bone-­ resorbing osteoclasts, marrow fibrosis, and cystic lesions that may contain fibrous tissue (brown tumors).

• Osteoporosis (unlike other osteoporotic disorders, hyperparathyroidism often

results in the preferential loss of cortical bone).

5.5.1.2 Hyperparathyroid Kidney Disease

• Kidney stones: they are usually calcium oxalate stones (usually recurrent and

difficult to manage medically).

• Nephrocalcinosis: deposition of calcium in the renal medulla (clinically evident

nephrocalcinosis rarely occurs, but a gradual loss of renal function is not uncommon).

• Renal impairment: [eGFR] <60 mL/min.

• Polydipsia and polyuria ← chronic hypercalcemia can also compromise the renal

concentrating ability. A number of symptoms and signs accompany hypercalcemia as follows:

• CNS effects: lethargy, depression, psychosis, ataxia, stupor, and coma.

• Neuromuscular effects: weakness, proximal myopathy, and hypertonia.

• Cardiovascular effects: hypertension, bradycardia (and eventually asystole), and

a shortened QT interval.

• Digestive effects: nausea, indigestion, vomiting, anorexia, constipation (sometimes

even—ileus ←↓ bowel motility ← hypercalcemia), peptic ulcers, pancreatitis.

• Eye findings such as band keratopathy.

• Systemic metastatic calcification: skin → itch; joints → chondrocalcinosis.

5.5.2 Primary Hyperparathyroidism Workup

5.5.2.1 Diagnosis of Primary Hyperparathyroidism

Parathyroid Glands

• ↑ Ionized calcium or total calcium; serum phosphorus is low-normal or low

(<3.5 mg/dL)

• Urinary calcium ↑; urinary phosphorus ↑

• ↑ of ALP level—reflecting high bone turnover

Hormonal Determinations

• ↑ Intact PTH level (an elevated level of PTH is clearly inappropriate in a hypercalcemic patient and establishes the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism);

in a patient with ↑ PTH level, there is no need to screen for metastatic malignancy, sarcoidosis, etc.

• ↑ 1,25(OH)2D3

I nvestigations Aimed at Determining the Presence of End-Organ Damage from Hypercalcemia for Clinical Decision-Making Reasons

X-rays, determinations of bone mineral density (BMD), renal function (U&E), and renal imaging (abdominal radiograph, ultrasound, CT scan for renal stones) are often obtained to determine whether operative intervention is indicated. Skeletal radiographs (lateral thoracolumbar spine, hands, and skull)—radiographic features include the following:

• Subperiosteal resorption, the most sensitive and specific radiologic finding of

osteitis fibrosa cystica. –– X-rays of the phalanges: showing classic subperiosteal resorption of cortical bone of phalanges. –– Skull X-ray: a similar process leads to a “salt and paper” appearance (← areas of demineralization alternating with areas of increased bone density).

• Bone cysts, usually multiple, which contain a brownish serous fluid, tend to

occur in the central medullary portions of the shafts of the metacarpals, ribs or pelvis. –– Osteoclastomas or “brown tumors,” composed of osteoclasts admixed with stromal cells and matrix are found most often in trabecular portions of the jaw, the long bones and ribs. Bone cysts or brown tumors may be evident as osteolytic lesion.

5.5 Primary Hyperparathyroidism

97

• Pathologic fractures.

• Dental films may disclose loss of the lamina dura of the teeth.

Renal tract ultrasound (calculi, nephrocalcinosis). BMD by DXA (dual X-ray absorptiometry) → osteoporosis.

5.5.2.3 Localization Studies of Abnormal Parathyroid Glands

This should only form part of a preoperative assessment and is not indicated in the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism (the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism is merely biochemical: ↑ Ca + ↑ PTH). The most successful procedures are 99mTc-sestamibi scanning coupled with SPECT/CT, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and ultrasound. Individually, each has a sensitivity of 60–80% in experienced hands. Used in combination, they are successful in at least 80% of cases. They are essential in the management of patients with recurrent or persistent hyperparathyroidism.

• Localization with two separate techniques (usually, US and 99mTc-sestamibi) is

imperative before minimally invasive parathyroidectomy.

• Otherwise, open bilateral neck exploration by an experienced surgeon is optimal

in the first instance.

5.5.3 Treatment

5.5.3.1 Surgery

The definitive treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism is parathyroidectomy. If localizing studies (such as sestamibi scan) clearly indicate a single abnormal gland and if intraoperative PTH testing is available, surgical management generally consists of unilateral exploration (minimally invasive surgery) of the neck with the removal of the single abnormal gland. Otherwise, a bilateral neck exploration in which all four glands are identified and all enlarged glands removed is preferred. In patients with hyperplasia, the preferred operation is partial parathyroidectomy (3½-gland parathyroidectomy), leaving a remnant sufficient to prevent hypocalcemia (perhaps with reimplantation of tissue in more accessible site).

Indications for Surgery in Primary Hyperparathyroidism

It is generally accepted that all patients with symptomatic hyperparathyroidism or evidence of end-organ damage should be considered for parathyroidectomy.

This would include the following: • • • •

Definite symptoms of hypercalcemia. Impaired renal function (eGFR < 60 ml/min). Renal stones (symptomatic or on radiograph). Parathyroid bone disease, especially osteitis fibrosa cystica; BMD DXA T-score <−2.5 SD; presence of vertebral fractures.

• Pancreatitis.

After parathyroidectomy a transitory postoperative hypocalcemia may appear:

• ← due to functional inhibition of the remnant parathyroid glands.

• ← due to the “hungry bone syndrome” ← avid uptake of calcium and phosphate

by the bones. –– → Treatment with calcium + vitamin D metabolites.

5.5.3.2 Conservative Management

There is no definitive medical therapy for primary hyperparathyroidism. Patients not managed with surgery require regular follow-up. Selective estrogen response modulator (SERM), Raloxifene®, bisphosphonates (Alendronat® etc.) have been tried but they do not have significant and or persistent effects on serum calcium or intact PTH levels. Calcimimetic agents (FDA-approved for the management of secondary hyperparathyroidism in patients with CKD on dialysis and of primary hyperparathyroidism as well in US) that activate the parathyroid CaSR may offer an alternative to surgery (for controlling hypercalcemia): for individuals who meet guidelines for surgical referral but who are too sick or unwilling to undergo surgery or in whom surgery has failed to cure their hyperparathyroidism: Cinacalcet® was shown to ↓/normalize serum [Ca2+] and raise serum phosphate with modest lowering of PTH levels in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism.

5.7 Hypocalcemia

99

Laboratory: Ca ↓/n, PTH ↑↑, vitamin D ↓↓. Treatment: Calcitriol or vitamin D analogs, calcium supplementation, phosphate restriction. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism occurs after prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism, if 1 or more glands act autonomously (e.g., with adenoma formation).

Hypocalcemia

Both PTH and 1,25(OH)2D maintain a normal serum calcium and are thus central to the defense against hypocalcemia. Thus, hypocalcemia disorders and chronic hypocalcemia can result from a failure to secrete PTH, altered responsiveness to PTH, a deficiency of vitamin D, or a resistance to vitamin D (see Table 5.2). Acute hypocalcemia is most often the consequence of an overwhelming challenge to the adaptive response such as rhabdomyolysis, in which a flood of phosphate from injured skeletal muscle floods the extracellular fluid.

5.7.2 Clinical Features

1. The clinical features of hypocalcemia are largely as a result of ↑ neuromuscular

excitability. In order of ↑ severity, these include the following:

(a) Tingling—especially of fingers, toes, or lips.

(b) Numbness—especially of fingers, toes, or lips.

100

Parathyroid Glands

(c) Cramps.

(d) Carpopedal spasm.

Tetany crisis is the hallmark of severe hypocalcemia ← tonic and painful contractions of the muscles; carpopedal spasm is the classic muscular component of tetany; although the hands are most typically involved, tetany can involve other muscle groups, including life-threatening spasm of laryngeal muscles. Tetany is not specific for hypocalcemia. It also occurs with hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, and respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation. Lesser degrees of neuromuscular excitability produce latent tetany which can be elicited by testing for the following: Chvostek sign: elicited by tapping the facial nerve about 2 cm anterior to the earlobe, just below the zygoma. A +ve result is indicated by twitching of the corner of the mouth. Trousseau sign: elicited by inflating a blood pressure cuff to about 20 mmHg above systolic pressure for 3 min. A positive response is carpal spasm.

(e) Stridor due to laryngospasm.

(f) Focal or generalized seizures; confusion.

2. Other manifestations of hypocalcemia:

(a) Hyperirritability, anxiety, depression, shortness of breath.

(b) Cardiac effects: prolongation of QT intervals; excitation–contraction coupling may be impaired, and refractory congestive heart failure is sometimes

observed, particularly in patients with underlying cardiac disease.

(c) Ophthalmologic effects: subcapsular cataract.

(d) Dermatologic effects: dry skin, coarse hair, brittle nails.

(e) In children: dental and enamel hypoplasia (if hypocalcemia is present during

the development of permanent teeth). Twenty percent of children with chronic hypocalcemia develop mental retardation.

3. In addition, there may be clinical signs and symptoms associated with the

underlying condition:

(a) Vitamin D deficiency may be associated with lethargy, generalized bone

pain, fractures, or proximal myopathy.

(b) Hypoparathyroidism can be accompanied by mental slowing and personality

disturbances as well as extrapyramidal signs due to calcifications of basal ganglia (development of a parkinsonism-like syndrome), cataracts, papilloedema, urolithiasis and renal impairment (see also later).

5.8 Hypoparathyroidism

It is an endocrine disease with low calcium and inappropriately low (insufficient) circulating PTH levels. Hypoparathyroidism (hypoPT) is the only major endocrine condition today, where the hormonal insufficiency in general is not treated by substitution of the missing hormone (PTH).

5.8 Hypoparathyroidism

101

Table 5.3 Etiology of hypoparathyroidism

• Surgical

• Autoimmune

• Other rare genetic conditions

• Deposition of metals (iron, copper, aluminum)

• Postradiation: radioactive iodine therapy for Graves’ disease

• Infiltrative: hemochromatosis, Wilson’s disease

• Idiopathic

The most common cause of chronic hypoPT is neck surgery, that is, secondary to thyroid or parathyroid surgery. HypoPT may have an autoimmune pathogenesis. In many such patients, the cause is a mutation in the autoimmune regulator of endocrine function (AIRE) gene (in which case it may be associated with primary adrenal insufficiency and mucocutaneous candidiasis in the setting of type I polyglandular autoimmune syndrome). A similar form of hypoparathyroidism can occur as an isolated finding, for example, with circulating autoantibodies to the CaSR. In addition, there are many other rare genetic conditions that can cause hypoPT either as part of a syndrome (e.g., DiGeorge syndrome—congenital absence of the parathyroids and thymus, characterized by thymic aplasia, immunodeficiency, and cardiac anomalies) or as an isolated endocrinopathy (Table 5.3).

5.8.1 Clinical Features

(in addition to those common to all forms of hypocalcemia, presented above) Complications and Renal Implications of Chronic HypoPT in Adults Patients with chronic HypoPT seem to have lower QoL, muscle complaints, including fatigue and weakness, more anxiety and tendency to depression. HypoPT has traditionally been associated with calcium-containing urolithiasis and renal impairment because of an increased calcium–phosphate product. Loss of renal PTH action decreases renal tubular reabsorption of calcium and excretion of phosphate causing hypercalciuria and hyperphosphatasemia respectively and resulting in an increased risk of renal complications, such as renal stones, renal insufficiency or nephrocalcinosis.

5.8.2 Laboratory Findings

• Hypocalcemia (↓ total calcium, ↓ ionized calcium) and hypercalciuria

• Hyperphosphatemia (because the phosphaturic effect of PTH is lost) and urinary

phosphate ↓

• Low or undetectable PTH level

ECG: prolongation of QT interval Electromyographically, tetany is typified by repetitive motor neuron action potentials, usually grouped as doublets.

5.9 Treatment of Hypocalcemia

• Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia is a medical emergency and demands urgent

treatment whatever the cause.

• Treatment of chronic hypocalcemia is more dependent on the cause.

5.9.1 Hypoparathyroidism Treatment

Objectives: the patient should be free of symptoms or signs of hypocalcemia and the target serum calcium should be at the low end of the reference range. The reason for this is that the renal retention of calcium brought about by PTH has been lost. Thus, any attempt to raise the plasma calcium well into the normal range is likely to result in unacceptable hypercalciuria, with the risk of nephrocalcinosis and renal stones. Standard treatment includes oral calcium salts and active vitamin D metabolites:

• Calcium supplements, orally—1–3 g of elemental calcium/day in divided

doses

• Activated vitamin D metabolites:

–– 1 α-calcidol (ALPHA-D3) [Alfacalcidiol is rapidly activated in the liver to 1,25(OH)2D]: 1–4 μg/day –– 1,25(OH)2vitD3 (calcitriol) (ROCALTROL): 1–3 μg/day

• An adequate vitamin D status: vitamin D supplementations in a daily dose of

400–800 IU

• Magnesium

PTH (1–84) is a not yet approved therapy but may improve quality of life.

5.9.2 Treatment of Acute Hypocalcemia

Patients with tetany or seizures require urgent IV treatment with calcium gluconate.

• Calcium gluconate 10% (1 ampoule = 10 ml of calcium gluconate −93 mg of

elemental calcium in 1 ml) by slow IV infusion, 1–2 amp.

• Diazepam, anxiolytics.

• Rebreathing into a paper bag.

• Oral calcium and a rapidly acting preparation of vitamin D (e.g., calcitriol)

should be started.

5.10 Vitamin D Deficiency

Results from one or more factors: inadequate sunlight exposure, inadequate nutrition (for example poor diet, especially vegetarians), malabsorption. Laboratory –– Low-normal/hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, low urine calcium –– ↑ PTH –– A low serum 25(OH)D level is diagnostic Treatment Treatment is best given in the form of calciferol to restore body stores, correct biochemical abnormalities, and heal bony abnormalities.

• Replacement doses of vitamin D: 800–2000 UI of calciferol/day

–– Vigantoletten 500–1000 UI (800–1000 UI/day in menopause) –– Vigantol drop (1 drop = 500 UI): 2–6 drops/day !!!!! <10,000 UI/day = safe

• Daily intake of CALCIUM: approximately 1000–1200 mg/day

Pseudohypoparathyroidism

Pseudohypoparathyroidism is a heritable disorder of target-organ unresponsiveness to PTH. Most commonly caused by autosomal dominant mutation of GNAS gene.

• PHP type IB: isolated resistance to PTH, which presents with the biochemical

features of hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

• PHP type IA has, in addition to these biochemical features, a characteristic

somatic phenotype known as Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (AHO). This comprises: short stature, round face, short neck, obesity, brachydactyly (short digits), shortened metatarsals and metacarpals, subcutaneous ossifications, and often reduced intelligence. Also TSH, LH, FSH, and GH signaling can be affected. Biochemical –– Hypocalcemia –– Hyperphosphatemia ↑ PTH and there is a markedly blunted response to the administration of PTH (Ellsworth–Howard test). Treatment The principles underlying the treatment of PHP are the same as those underlying hypoparathyroidism.

5.12 Osteoporosis

Bone Turnover In order to ensure that bone can undertake its mechanical and metabolic functions, it is in a constant state of turnover.

• Osteoclasts—derived from the monocytic cells; resorb bone.

• Osteoblasts—derived from the fibroblast-like cells; make bone.

• Osteocytes—buried osteoblasts; sense mechanical strain in bone.

Bone Mass During Life During pubertal skeletal growth, bone mass strengthens rapidly and then follows a period of stabilization in early adult life. After the age of ≈40, bone mass gradually lowers in both sexes. Women, however, register a more rapid bone mass loss after the menopause (around 10% of skeletal mass). This women-characteristic bone loss associated with menopause, on the one hand, and the higher peak bone mass acquisition in males, on the other hand explains why osteoporosis and its associated fractures are more common in ♀. Osteoporosis is a metabolic bone disease, characterized by the following:

• reduction in the amount of bony tissue within the skeleton

• loss of structural integrity of the internal architecture of the bone

–– Osteoporotic bone is at high risk of fracture, even after trivial injury. The term primary osteoporosis denotes reduced bone mass and fractures in postmenopausal women (postmenopausal osteoporosis) or in older men and women due to age-related factors. The term secondary osteoporosis refers to bone loss resulting from specific clinical disorders, such as thyrotoxicosis, glucocorticoid excess, and many others (Table 5.4). The most common osteoporotic fractures are those of the hip, wrist (Colles’), and compression fractures of vertebral bodies. Note: Any fracture, other than those affecting fingers, toes, or face, which is caused by a fall from standing height or less is called a fragility (low-trauma) fracture, and underlying osteoporosis should be considered. Patients suffering such a fracture should be considered for investigation and/or treatment for osteoporosis.

5. Inflammatory conditions:

(a) Rheumatoid arthritis

(b) Cystic fibrosis

6. Medications

Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists, cyclosporine, systemic glucocorticoids

5.12.2 Presentation of Osteoporosis

• Usually clinically silent until an acute fracture.

–– Typical vertebral fracture: Sudden episode of well-localized pain. Pain may initially require bed rest but gradually subsides over 4–8 weeks; even after this time, there may be residual pain at the fracture site. Following vertebral fracture, a patient may be left with persistent back pain, kyphosis, or height loss. –– Peripheral fractures after low trauma are also more common in

5.12.3 Osteoporosis Workup

Note: Osteoporosis does not cause generalized skeletal pain!!!!

Osteoporosis Workup

The diagnosis of osteoporosis may be obvious in patients who have sustained fragility fractures, but noninvasive methods to estimate BMD are required to identify high-risk patients who have not yet sustained a fracture. BMD is a highly significant predictor of fracture risk.

1. Bone densitometry. In order to identify the presence of T score-defined osteoporosis, it is important to measure BMD appropriately (Table 5.5). This is usually carried out at the hip and lumbar spine, using dual-energy X-ray

absorptiometry (DXA), which offers the most precise measurement for the least amount of radiation exposure. Measurement of BMD with DXA is considered the gold standard for the diagnosis of osteoporosis. Results: absolute value in g/cm2.

Interpretation of results: bone mass is quoted in terms of the number of SD from an expected mean. The most useful way of expressing this is as T scores:

(a) T-score: number of SD patient’s BMD above or below average BMD of

young–adult reference population used for diagnosis.

(b) Z-score: number of SD patient’s BMD above or below average BMD of age

and gender-matched reference population; used to suggest further evaluation. A reduction of one SD in bone density will approximately double the risk of fracture.

2. Lateral thoracic and lumbar spine X-rays are useful for detecting vertebral

fractures and for their follow-up.

3. Use of fracture risk algorithms is now available to determine individuals’ fracture risk (e.g., http://www.shef.ac.uk/FRAX). FRAX is a diagnostic tool that

integrates clinical risk factors and BMD at the femoral neck to calculate the 10-year probability of hip fracture and the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture. Such an approach can help tune therapies to those patients at heightened risk of fracture.

4. Laboratory studies (employed to exclude secondary osteoporosis): ESR, FBC,

ALT and AST, urea and creatinine levels, serum calcium, phosphate, ALP, TSH, FT4 ± PTH, urinary free cortisol level, testosterone and gonadotropin levels (FSH, LH), ±25(OH) vitamin D, serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) and urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP), anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies (if any suggestion of coeliac disease), and/or other investigations for specific diseases. Note: It is helpful to target these investigations at those people who have a significantly lower than expected bone mass for their age (Z score <−2).

5.12.4 Treatment

Therapeutic Goals ↑ BMD and ↓ risk for fractures In addition to pharmacological treatments aimed at reducing fracture risk, it must be remembered that non-pharmacological measures are also important. Thus, it is prudent to minimize the risk of falling by adjusting the home environment and reviewing the need for medications, such as hypnotics and antihypertensives, for instance.

5.12 Osteoporosis

5.12.4.1 Lifestyle Measures

• Encourage weight-bearing exercise (e.g., leg-strengthening exercises, lower-­

impact exercise, e.g., walking outdoors for 20 min 3× weekly → may reduce fracture risk).

• Falls prevention and hip protectors.

• Encourage well-balanced diet.

Ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D intake: optimal intake of calcium: ≈1000–1200 mg/day; vitamin D supplementation should be added if necessary; proteins.

5.12.4.2 Pharmacologic Agents

• Antiresorptives:

–– Bisphosphonates –– Calcitonin –– SERM (Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators) –– Hormone replacement therapy (estrogen) –– Denosumab (monoclonal antibody directed against RANKL)

Bisphosphonates (Alendronate, Risedronate, Zoledronic Acid)

Weekly (PO), daily (PO), monthly (PO), 3-monthly (IV), and annual (IV) preparations are available. Oral bisphosphonates should be taken on an empty stomach, and 30–60 min (dependent on drug) should pass prior to additional oral intake. Side effects: GI disturbance, including nausea and esophagitis, are common; osteonecrosis of the jaw is a very rare side effect; there is a possible association between atypical subtrochanteric femoral fractures in patients who have taken several years of bisphosphonates.

• Osteo-anabolic (bone-forming) agents:

–– Recombinant human PTH (1–34) (Teriparatide): given in daily subcutaneous doses has been shown to increase BMD and reduce fracture risk –– Strontium ranelate
